title: Tender Is the Night
description: Fitzgerald's most ambitious novel: the Divers on the Riviera, and the destruction of a marriage by money and illness.
plot_or_argument: Dick Diver, a brilliant young psychiatrist, marries his patient Nicole Warren, whose family's wealth has bought her cure; the novel follows their marriage across the Riviera, Paris and Zurich, Dick's decline into drink and obscurity, his affair with the young actress Rosemary Hoyt, and Nicole's recovery and departure.
narrative_structure: Originally in three books, with a flashback structure; Fitzgerald reordered it in 1951.
principal_characters: Dick Diver; Nicole Warren Diver; Rosemary Hoyt; Tommy Barban; Baby Warren; Abe North
historical_context: The American expatriate Riviera of the 1920s, the psychiatric clinic, and the Wall Street crash that ended the party.
literary_significance: Tender Is the Night is Fitzgerald's most ambitious novel and one of the great American studies of marriage and money: its portrait of the destruction of a gifted man by the wealth that cured his wife is unmatched in American fiction.

title: The Sun Also Rises
description: The definitive novel of the Lost Generation: Paris, Pamplona and Jake Barnes's unhealed wound.
plot_or_argument: Jake Barnes, an American journalist in Paris left impotent by a war wound, loves Lady Brett Ashley, who loves him but cannot be with him; the novel follows their circle through the Paris cafés to the fiesta at Pamplona, where Brett seduces the young matador Pedro Romero, and ends with Brett's telegram calling Jake back to Madrid.
narrative_structure: Three parts: Paris, Pamplona, Madrid, in a first-person narrative.
principal_characters: Jake Barnes; Lady Brett Ashley; Robert Cohn; Mike Campbell; Bill Gorton; Pedro Romero
historical_context: Paris in the 1920s, the expatriate colony, the fiesta of San Fermín at Pamplona, and the post-war generation that had lost its faith.
literary_significance: The Sun Also Rises defined the Lost Generation and made Hemingway the voice of his age: its understated prose, its code of grace under pressure and its portrait of a wounded generation made it the decade's definitive novel.

title: A Farewell to Arms
description: The finest American novel of the First World War: an ambulance driver, the retreat from Caporetto and a love affair that ends in loss.
plot_or_argument: Frederic Henry, an American ambulance lieutenant in the Italian army, falls in love with Catherine Barkley, a British nurse; he is wounded at the front, recovers in Milan, returns to the retreat from Caporetto, deserts after the battle police shoot his comrades, and escapes with Catherine to Switzerland, where she dies in childbirth with the baby.
narrative_structure: Five books with a coda, in a first-person narrative.
principal_characters: Frederic Henry; Catherine Barkley; Rinaldi; the priest; Helen Ferguson; Miss Van Campen
historical_context: The Italian front of 1915–18, the retreat from Caporetto, Milan in wartime, and the armistice.
literary_significance: A Farewell to Arms is the finest American novel of the First World War and the book that made Hemingway a major writer: its prose, its love story and its ending — 'the world breaks everyone' — made it one of the permanent American novels of the century.

title: In Our Time
description: The book that made the modern American short story: 'Indian Camp', 'Big Two-Hearted River' and the ice-fishing interludes.
plot_or_argument: The collection alternates between short stories — 'Indian Camp', 'The Doctor and the Doctor's Wife', 'The End of Something', 'The Three-Day Blow', 'Soldier's Home', 'Cat in the Rain' and 'Big Two-Hearted River' — and brief prose vignettes of war, bullfighting and crime.
narrative_structure: Fifteen stories alternating with fifteen short prose interludes.
principal_characters: Nick Adams; the doctor; the Indian father; Krebs; the bullfighter
historical_context: The Michigan woods of Hemingway's childhood, the First World War, the Greco-Turkish war and the bullfighting of Spain.
literary_significance: In Our Time created the modern American short story: its iceberg theory — the meaning withheld from the surface — its prose and its structure of stories and interludes made it the founding collection of the American short story in the century.

title: The Sound and the Fury
description: Faulkner's masterpiece and one of the most formally daring novels of the century: the fall of the Compson family.
plot_or_argument: The Compsons of Jefferson, Mississippi — the alcoholic Quentin, the idiot Benjy, the lost Candace (Caddy) and the brutal Jason — decline over thirty years, and the novel tells the same events four times: through Benjy's associative memory, Quentin's suicidal day at Harvard in 1910, Jason's cynical narration, and finally the third-person account of Dilsey, the Black servant who holds the family together.
narrative_structure: Four sections: Benjy's, Quentin's, Jason's and a third-person section centred on Dilsey.
principal_characters: Benjy Compson; Quentin Compson; Jason Compson; Caddy Compson; Dilsey; Miss Quentin; Herbert Head
historical_context: Jefferson, Mississippi, in 1910 and 1928, the decline of the Southern aristocracy, the Black servant community and the burden of the Southern past.
literary_significance: The Sound and the Fury is Faulkner's masterpiece and one of the great novels of the century: its four narratives, its rendering of idiocy and memory, and its portrait of the Compsons gave American literature its most radical experiment in form and its deepest study of the Southern past.

title: As I Lay Dying
description: The Bundren family's journey to bury Addie: fifty-nine monologues, and the blackest comedy in American fiction.
plot_or_argument: Addie Bundren dies and her husband Anse and five children set out to carry her body to Jefferson for burial; the journey takes nine days, the coffin is nearly lost in a flooded river and a fire, and each member of the family narrates in turn, revealing their own motives and the family's terrible poverty.
narrative_structure: Fifty-nine monologues by fifteen narrators over nine days.
principal_characters: Addie Bundren; Anse Bundren; Cash Bundren; Darl Bundren; Jewel Bundren; Dewey Dell; Vardaman
historical_context: The rural Mississippi of the 1920s, the poor white farming family, and the funeral customs of the South.
literary_significance: As I Lay Dying is the blackest comedy in American fiction and one of the great experimental novels of the century: its fifty-nine monologues and its journey structure made it the most formally perfect of Faulkner's novels.

title: Light in August
description: Faulkner's great novel of race and the American outsider: Joe Christmas, Lena Grove and the lynching.
plot_or_argument: Lena Grove, a pregnant country girl, walks to Jefferson in search of the father of her child; there she crosses the path of Joe Christmas, a man of uncertain racial identity who is suspected of murdering his lover Joanna Burden and is hunted down and lynched. The novel interweaves their stories with that of the disgraced minister Gail Hightower.
narrative_structure: Three interwoven stories in a chronological-but-delayed narrative.
principal_characters: Joe Christmas; Lena Grove; Gail Hightower; Joanna Burden; Byron Bunch; Lucas Burch; Doc Hines
historical_context: Jefferson, Mississippi, in the 1920s, the racial violence of the South, and the burden of the Calvinist past.
literary_significance: Light in August is Faulkner's great novel of race and one of the most powerful American novels of the century: its portrait of Joe Christmas, its treatment of lynching and its counterpoint of Lena Grove's journey made it the moral centre of the Southern Renaissance.

title: Absalom, Absalom!
description: Faulkner's most ambitious novel: Thomas Sutpen, his hundred-year design, and the curse of the Southern past.
plot_or_argument: Quentin Compson, at Harvard in 1910, is told by his father and by Rosa Coldfield the story of Thomas Sutpen, who came to Jefferson in 1833, built a plantation called Sutpen's Hundred, married Ellen Coldfield, and was destroyed by the return of his part-Black son Charles Bon and the refusal of his white son Henry to accept him.
narrative_structure: Nine sections narrated by four narrators reconstructing the Sutpen story across decades.
principal_characters: Thomas Sutpen; Quentin Compson; Rosa Coldfield; Charles Bon; Henry Sutpen; Judith Sutpen; Shreve McCannon
historical_context: The antebellum South, the Civil War, and the racial and familial guilt that the Southern present inherits.
literary_significance: Absalom, Absalom! is Faulkner's most ambitious novel and one of the most complex in American literature: its multiple narrators, its reconstruction of a story that can never be known and its treatment of race and the Southern past made it the summit of the Southern Renaissance.

title: Go Down, Moses
description: The McCaslin family across a century: slavery, the land and the bear, and Faulkner's most moving book.
plot_or_argument: The seven stories follow the McCaslin and Beauchamp families from the 1850s to the 1940s — the hunting of the great bear Old Ben, the discovery of the family's slave heritage, the death of the old hunter Sam Fathers, and the return of Lucas Beauchamp's grandson — in a book about the land, race and inheritance.
narrative_structure: Seven stories spanning a century, from 'Was' to 'Go Down, Moses'.
principal_characters: Ike McCaslin; Lucas Beauchamp; Sam Fathers; Old Ben; Boon Hogganbeck; Carothers McCaslin
historical_context: The Mississippi wilderness and its destruction by the lumber companies, the legacy of slavery, and the Southern hunting tradition.
literary_significance: Go Down, Moses is Faulkner's most moving book and the finest treatment of race and inheritance in American fiction: 'The Bear' is one of the great American stories, and the book's century-long family chronicle made the McCaslins the equal of the Compsons.

title: Look Homeward, Angel
description: The great lyric novel of American appetite: Eugene Gant, the small Southern town and the hunger to escape.
plot_or_argument: Eugene Gant grows up in the boarding house of his mother Eliza in Altamont, North Carolina, among his stonecutter father Gant's rhetoric, his siblings' deaths and the town's gossip, and escapes to university and the North; the novel ends with his brother Ben's death and Eugene's departure.
narrative_structure: Three parts following Eugene from childhood to departure, in a lyric autobiographical narrative.
principal_characters: Eugene Gant; Eliza Gant; W. O. Gant; Ben Gant; Helen Gant; Luke Gant; Laura James
historical_context: The small-town South of the 1900s and 1910s, the boarding house, the stonecutting trade, and the First World War.
literary_significance: Look Homeward, Angel is the great lyric novel of American appetite and the first book of the Southern Renaissance: its torrent of names and memories, its portrait of the Gant family and its hunger for experience changed the possibilities of American prose.

title: Of Time and the River
description: Wolfe's second novel: Eugene Gant at Harvard, in New York and in Europe, and the hunger that cannot be satisfied.
plot_or_argument: Eugene Gant goes to Harvard to study playwriting, teaches in New York, travels to England and France, falls in love with Esther Jack, and returns to America — in a torrent of memory, hunger and loss that continues the story begun in Look Homeward, Angel.
narrative_structure: A long autobiographical narrative in many chapters, continuing Look Homeward, Angel.
principal_characters: Eugene Gant; Esther Jack; Francis Starwick; Joel Pierce; Robert Weaver
historical_context: Harvard in the 1920s, New York, the expatriate Europe of the period, and the American hunger for experience.
literary_significance: Of Time and the River is the great American novel of hunger and the most expansive autobiographical novel in American literature: its torrent of prose made Wolfe the most discussed young novelist of the 1930s.

title: Flowering Judas
description: Porter's first collection and the most perfectly finished American stories of the period.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'María Concepción', 'Virgin Violeta', 'He', 'Magic', 'Rope' and the title story 'Flowering Judas', in which Laura, an American revolutionary in Mexico, is haunted by the betrayal of a young Indian prisoner and by the Judas tree of her garden.
narrative_structure: Six stories, mostly set in Mexico and Texas.
principal_characters: Laura; Braggioni; María Concepción; Violeta; Rosaleen
historical_context: Mexico in the 1920s, the revolutionary years, and Porter's own years as a journalist and revolutionary in Mexico.
literary_significance: Flowering Judas is the most perfectly finished American short-story collection of the period: its title story is one of the great American stories, and the collection made Porter the finest stylist of the American short story.

title: Pale Horse, Pale Rider
description: Porter's finest book: the influenza epidemic, the South of her childhood, and 'Noon Wine'.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Old Mortality', 'Noon Wine' and the title novella 'Pale Horse, Pale Rider', in which Miranda, a young newspaperwoman in Denver in 1918, falls in love with a soldier and nearly dies of influenza in the epidemic that killed more Americans than the war.
narrative_structure: Three novellas in different settings, from the South to the Texas farm to Denver in 1918.
principal_characters: Miranda; Adam Barclay; Mr Thompson; Mr Helton; Mr Hatch; Amy
historical_context: The influenza epidemic of 1918, the American South of Porter's childhood, and the Texas farm of 'Noon Wine'.
literary_significance: Pale Horse, Pale Rider is Porter's finest book and one of the great American novellas of the century: its title story is the definitive literary record of the 1918 influenza, and 'Noon Wine' is one of the finest American stories ever written.

title: A Curtain of Green
description: Welty's first collection: 'A Worn Path', 'Why I Live at the P.O.' and the comic-grotesque South.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'A Worn Path', 'Why I Live at the P.O.', 'Petrified Man', 'The Hitch-Hikers', 'Powerhouse' and 'A Curtain of Green' — stories of the Mississippi small town, the rural poor and the comic eccentric.
narrative_structure: Seventeen stories set in the Mississippi small town and countryside.
principal_characters: Phoenix Jackson; the sister; Leota; Powerhouse; the hitch-hikers
historical_context: The Mississippi of Welty's childhood in the 1930s, the Depression, and the small-town South.
literary_significance: A Curtain of Green is the finest first collection of American stories of the period: 'A Worn Path' and 'Why I Live at the P.O.' are permanent, and Welty's comic-grotesque vision made her the great comic writer of the Southern Renaissance.

title: The Optimist's Daughter
description: Welty's finest novel: a judge's daughter, a funeral in Mississippi and the recovery of memory.
plot_or_argument: Laurel McKelva Hand returns to Mount Salus, Mississippi, for the death of her father, the Judge; she confronts his much younger second wife Fay and, in the ruins of the family house, comes to terms with her parents, her dead husband and her own memory.
narrative_structure: Four parts, moving from the hospital in New Orleans to the return to Mount Salus.
principal_characters: Laurel McKelva Hand; Judge McKelva; Fay McKelva; Miss Adele Courtland; Dr Courtland
historical_context: The Mississippi small town of the 1960s, the family house and the burial ground, and the memory of the 1920s.
literary_significance: The Optimist's Daughter won the Pulitzer Prize and is Welty's finest novel: its portrait of a woman coming to terms with her parents and her past is one of the great American novels of memory.

title: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
description: The greatest Southern novel of adolescence: a deaf mute in a Georgia mill town and the four people who need him.
plot_or_argument: John Singer, a deaf mute, is the confidant of four people in a Georgia mill town — Mick Kelly, a young girl who loves music; Jake Blount, a drunken radical; Dr Copeland, a Black physician; and Biff Brannon, the café owner — and when his friend Spiros Antonapoulos dies, Singer kills himself and each of the four is left alone.
narrative_structure: Three parts following the four characters around Singer.
principal_characters: John Singer; Mick Kelly; Jake Blount; Dr Copeland; Biff Brannon; Antonapoulos
historical_context: A Georgia mill town in the late 1930s, the Depression, and the isolation of the small Southern town.
literary_significance: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter is the greatest Southern novel of adolescence and one of the great American novels of loneliness: written at twenty-three, it made McCullers the youngest of the Southern writers and gave American fiction one of its permanent portraits of isolation.

title: The Member of the Wedding
description: The great American novel of a girl's growing up: Frankie Addams, her brother's wedding, and the end of childhood.
plot_or_argument: Frankie Addams, twelve, is desperate to belong to her brother Jarvis's wedding and plans to go away with the couple; the wedding comes and goes without her, and the novel ends with her recovered from the crisis, changed and about to move.
narrative_structure: Three parts over the days before and after the wedding.
principal_characters: Frankie Addams; Berenice Sadie Brown; John Henry West; Jarvis; Janice
historical_context: A Georgia town in the 1940s, the kitchen of the Addams house and the Black servant Berenice's kitchen.
literary_significance: The Member of the Wedding is one of the great American novels of growing up: its portrait of Frankie, its dialogue and its title have made it a permanent American classic and a landmark of the Southern Renaissance.

title: Poems (Auden, 1930)
description: The book that made Auden the leader of his generation: 'Consider', 'The Watershed' and the clipped public voice of the thirties.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Consider this and in our time', 'The Watershed', 'The Secret Agent', '1929' and the early lyrics of the industrial north and the public school — the poems that gave the decade its voice.
narrative_structure: Thirty poems, mostly short lyrics, in a clipped public manner.
literary_form: Poetry collection (hand-printed by Stephen Spender, 1928; published by Faber, 1930)
historical_context: The England of the late 1920s: the General Strike, the industrial north, the public school and the new consciousness of class and crisis.
literary_significance: Auden's Poems made him the leader of his generation and the central English poet of the 1930s: its clipped, journalistic line, its parable and its political unease invented the poetic idiom of the decade.

title: The Orators: An English Study
description: Auden's most experimental book: a prose-and-verse anatomy of the English public school, the leader and the enemy.
plot_or_argument: The book is in three parts — an address to a leader, a journal of a school and a series of odes — and mixes prose, verse, parody and private joke in a study of the English ruling class, the cult of the hero and the sickness of the public school.
narrative_structure: Three parts: an address, a journal and six odes.
principal_characters: The Airman; the Leader; the pupils; the uncle
historical_context: The English public school of the 1920s, the political crisis of 1931–32, and the new psychology of the leader and the group.
literary_significance: The Orators is Auden's most experimental book and one of the key texts of the thirties: its mixture of prose and verse, its anatomy of the English ruling class and its diagnosis of the cult of the leader made it the period's most original political poem.

title: Look, Stranger!
description: Auden's finest single collection: 'Stop all the clocks', 'Look, stranger', 'Musée des Beaux Arts' and the love poems.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone', 'Look, stranger, at this island now', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'The Dog Beneath the Skin' lyrics, 'O what is that sound', 'Lullaby' and 'May with its light behaving' — the public poem, the love poem and the elegy together.
narrative_structure: Thirty poems in varied forms, from the ballad to the ode.
literary_form: Poetry collection (US title On This Island)
historical_context: The England of 1935–36, the rise of fascism, the Spanish Civil War, and Auden's love for Michael Yates and his engagement with the political crisis.
literary_significance: Look, Stranger! is Auden's finest single collection and the summit of the thirties poem: 'Stop all the clocks' is one of the best-known elegies in English, 'Musée des Beaux Arts' the definitive poem about suffering, and 'Look, stranger' the great English poem of the island.
